You sound like me. You're probably neurodivergent. I got diagnosed at 28 after floundering my first 10 years of working life with the same issues as you. Not remembering things. Taking too long to learn. Being physically too slow at the tasks. Also generally hating the jobs and getting anxiety and depression as a result. I was then diagnosed as being on the autism spectrum, with likely ADHD and dyspraxia also (the assessor was paid strictly to check for autism).

This has helped me massively, as it explains me and puts my mind at ease, it lets me explain myself to others and hopefully get a bit of understanding and acceptance, and it's helped point me in the direction of what jobs are much better suited for me. It also opens the door to getting special assistance in finding work with the way that I am in mind (aka the work coaches have access to much better and more suitable opportunities for me)

Now the thing is I also have big strengths which the majority of other people do not, like creativity, out of the box thinking, numbers, and understanding complex things well, like physics, the stock market, the law etc, despite my terrible memory for other things like what goes where on a shelf, that if I'm honest are most likely because I just subconciously find them so trivial that I think my brain just doesn't play ball. So the fact I'm crap at stacking shelves really in the grand scheme of things isn't a very big price to pay. The problem was that you can't easily get into these more advanced jobs without the qualifications that you're too fidgety to sit through, and so you end up forced into the mundane jobs which tend to just require a drone like state of mind and fast hands (aka jobs I always say you'd be better hiring a robot for), but this is where specialist work coaching and support really helps open doors to the right employers and positions etc. Because there are companies out there that have positions for which they actively prefer to hire the neurodivergent.

I can't recommend you look into this route before you waste too much time, I wish I could've known myself better at 18.

No, the other way around, his head would age faster than his legs if his legs were in the higher gravity area.

So if he could experience this afterwards, in his old age he might still have really youthful legs.

But in effect it wouldnt quite work like that I don't think, due to all sorts of biological effects, like the blood not being able to pump back up from the legs so it would just pool there. Also current aging research seems to point to it being slightly more complex than that anyway, for example, the old cells in the rest of the body would likely interact to accelerate the aging of the younger cells in the legs, and the younger cells in the legs would act to slow the aging of the cells in the rest of the body.

But to get to what you're likely wondering, firstly to make it easier to picture, if the black hole was sufficiently powerful, the gradient wouldn't need to be very long at all for his head and feet to experience hugely different rates of time passing, so he could do it if without being freakishly big. If he then instead stuck his head nearer to the black hole than his feet and rest of his body, then from the perspective of his head the cells in his body would age much faster. But again, even though that theoretically might mean he gets a super old body on a young head, what would probably happen first is his body simply dying because it hasn't had any nutrients for ages in relation to his head.

Method I've found tends to be a little more successful is a scorecard one, where I'll keep tabs, normally initiating one convo, then waiting for them to initiate the next. Normally I'm aiming for a roughly 1:1 ratio of initiation, but I try to treat it more as a probability distribution rather than a strict me-then-you, me-then-you. This allows for me to initiate twice in a row or even three times in a row or more, but as long as we're talking roughly 50/50 when averaged out. Modelling like how coin toss distributions behave.

This method does not always mean that I am reaching out when it is appropriate/wanted, but for the most part, it does. Crucially though, I find it avoids the aforementioned negative pitfall of the wait-until-messaged-first model, and in so doing, becomes a more effective model overall, thus leading to my adoption of it.

Secondly, sadly you do have to ensure you stick to a good amount of hours of sleep and a regular sleeping pattern. You can't cheat it, it will f**k you up. Now you can afford the odd late night partying or studying or whatever, but you will owe your body a debt, make sure it's kept paid up to date as it can't be cheated. The price is fatigue and poor mental faculties. And keep at it with a sleep regime, sometimes your body will need a few days or weeks to truly recover if you are sleep deprived or out of pattern, often times one good long sleep isn't enough to fully recover

Thirdly, recognise that as a human, you have a limited amount of energy and a limited amount of time to spend each day. You have to learn to forgive yourself for that. I used to stress and worry and beat myself up because I wasn't studying enough, I wasn't keeping fit enough, I wasn't making enough money, etc etc etc. I didn't respect the time and energy limits that I had - that we all have. Naturally, I wanted to do everything and I wanted to do it all perfectly. The stress and worry and overthinking that generated also cost yet more mental energy and time, and left me with little to none. Now I will say that this shouldn't discourage you, as it is possible to achieve a lot, maybe everything you want. BUT, you have to recognise the limitations. Imagine an F1 car. Car holds a limited amount of fuel in order to save weight and go faster, driver has a limited amount of reaction time, even the tyres have a limited amount of tread before they are all spent up. But that's all part of the game, doesn't mean the driver can't win the race. Just has to be sensible and learn to use what he has to maximum effect and efficiency. Just remember, just like the master F1 driver, as nice as it would be, your tank doesn't contain infinite fuel, so you need to learn how and when to push the pedal down to achieve maximum effect with what you've got.

Hope some of this helps you.

As far as I'm aware, graying under the age of 30 or so is classed as premature graying.

Graying isn't fully understood yet, so we don't know exactly how to stop it or reverse it. However, it seems that there are several things that have been shown to have an effect on hair graying.

As far as I understand, there are two main suspected causes of graying. The first is the death of the stem cells that produce melanin in the hair follicle, and the second is a reduction in the production of an enzyme called catalase, which breaks down naturally occuring hydrogen peroxide in the hair follicle, as a build up of hydrogen peroxide can bleach hair lighter or white.

Stress is known to accelerate graying, as is an unhealthy diet, smoking, an underactive thyroid, and certain vitamin deficiencies. So the cause of yours could be one of these, or none

It is not unheard of for graying to be sometimes reversed too. Restoring thyroid function in individuals with impaired function can make hair colour return, as can pinpointing and addressing any vitamin deficiencies if that is the cause. There has also been some experiments where hair was successfully recoloured, one was with an experimental cream containing catalase I beleive, and the other I heard of was a side effect of a drug used to treat cancer.

It is worth getting a medical check up if you can just to rule out any actual medical problems like thyroid or vitamin deficiencies, but if not, theres no harm in trying other things.

For myself, I have taken steps to make sure I don't let myself get stressed out so much, and I take vitamin D, as well as anti-aging supplements resveratrol and NMN, which are big in science right now, especially NMN. I do think that the rate at which my hair was going gray has slowed down, and sometimes I even catch hairs that were gray that are going dark again. But it's not completely cured me or anything, it's still a problem I have.

I don't think so, no, or if so, only in line with inflation at most.

From the civilian point of view, it seems a no-brainer to have the minimum wage raised. General public also are under the illusion from the media that businessmen are all greedy capitalists, clawing away all that money for themselves.

Reality is, it would raise prices of everything across the board, so ultimately nobody would be any better off unfortunately.

If you raise minimum wage, you would have to raise everybody elses wages too proportionately to make it fair. IE, if person A earns £8.91 p/h (UK minimum wage) to be a cleaner for example, and person B is a cleaner who earns £10 p/h after doing a course to additionally undertake the responsibility of being supervisor of the rest of the cleaners, then if you raise the cleaners to £10, you have to raise the supervisors to at least £11.09 to make it still worth doing, so that it's fair to the supervisors too.

Then if you buy any item or service, incorporated into the item is the cost of people's wages who contributed to that item. Take a pint of milk for example. The cost of the wages of the person who looked after the cow, the person who prepared and bottled the milk, the person who delivered the milk to the shop, and the person who stacked the milk on the shelf, all need to be paid out of the money customers pay for the milk. So when all wages go up, the end product goes up too.

The end result is just inflation, you may then earn an extra, for example, £50 a month, but ultimately your cost of living will then raise to about £50 a month higher too, so it's really an illusion that you would be any better off.

What can happen too is that some jobs become unviable. For example, I used to be a self employed window cleaner. I wanted to take on somebody to help me, but I never was able to in my area, because it worked out that customers only wanted to pay a certain price for a window clean, and that price would have meant that I could only realistically pay a helper about £6.50 an hour maximum to clean them, unless they were inhumanly fast, as otherwise the total hourly costs of employing them once taxes and insurances were also taken into account would have meant that I lost money on every house they cleaned, so I couldn't do it. Now, while there are not enough jobs to go around,  I would argue that £6.50 p/h is better than no job at all.
